skills.title: Decimal Place Value
skills.summary: A decimal point separates whole ones from parts of one. The first place after the point is tenths, the next is hundredths, then thousandths. Each place is one tenth the size of the place to its left, just like the whole-number places but going the other way.
objectives: Name the place of a digit after the decimal point (tenths, hundredths, thousandths).
State the value of a digit based on its decimal place.
Write a decimal as a fraction over 10, 100, or 1000, and back.

skills.title: Reading and Comparing Decimals
skills.summary: To compare decimals, compare the digits place by place from the left, just like whole numbers. Extra zeros on the right do not change a decimal's value, so 0.7 and 0.70 are equal. A longer decimal is not automatically larger.
objectives: Read a decimal aloud using place-value names.
Compare two decimals by aligning place values.
Explain why trailing zeros do not change a decimal's value.

skills.title: Fractions and Decimals
skills.summary: A fraction and a decimal can name the same amount. Tenths and hundredths convert directly (0.7 = 7/10), and other fractions convert by making an equivalent fraction over 10 or 100, or by dividing the numerator by the denominator.
objectives: Convert a fraction with denominator 10 or 100 to a decimal and back.
Convert common fractions such as 1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, and 1/8 to decimals.
Write a terminating decimal as a fraction in simplest form.

skills.title: Adding and Subtracting Decimals
skills.summary: To add or subtract decimals, line up the decimal points so that tenths add to tenths and hundredths to hundredths, then add or subtract as with whole numbers and bring the decimal point straight down.
objectives: Add two decimals by aligning place values.
Subtract one decimal from another by aligning place values.
Explain why the decimal points must be lined up before adding or subtracting.

skills.title: Multiplying and Dividing Decimals
skills.summary: To multiply decimals, multiply as with whole numbers, then place the decimal point so the answer has as many decimal places as the two factors combined. To divide a decimal by a whole number, divide as usual and bring the decimal point straight up.
objectives: Multiply a decimal by a whole number.
Multiply two decimals and place the decimal point using the total number of decimal places.
Divide a decimal by a whole number.

skills.title: The Meaning of Percent
skills.summary: Percent means per hundred. A percent is a fraction with denominator 100, so 25% means 25 out of 100, which is the fraction 25/100 and the decimal 0.25. This lets you switch freely among percents, fractions, and decimals.
objectives: Explain that percent means per hundred.
Write a percent as a fraction over 100 and as a decimal.
Write a decimal or a fraction over 100 as a percent.

skills.title: Finding a Percent of a Number
skills.summary: To find a percent of a number, write the percent as a decimal (or a fraction) and multiply. For example, 25% of 80 is 0.25 times 80, which is 20. This is how discounts, tips, and shares of a total are calculated.
objectives: Write a percent as a decimal to prepare for multiplication.
Find a percent of a whole number.
Apply percent-of-a-number to a real situation such as a discount.

skills.title: Converting Fractions, Decimals, and Percents
skills.summary: Fractions, decimals, and percents are three ways to write the same amount. A decimal times 100 is a percent, a percent over 100 is a fraction, and a fraction can become a decimal by division. Being able to move among all three makes comparing and reasoning easier.
objectives: Convert between any two of fraction, decimal, and percent forms.
Compare numbers written in different forms by converting to a common form.
Choose a convenient form for a given situation.

skills.title: Rounding Decimals
skills.summary: Rounding a decimal replaces it with a nearby simpler value to a chosen place. Look at the digit just to the right of the rounding place: if it is 5 or more, round up; if it is less than 5, round down (keep the digit as it is).
objectives: Round a decimal to the nearest whole number.
Round a decimal to a given decimal place.
Explain the rule for deciding whether to round up or down.

skills.title: Finding the Whole
skills.summary: Sometimes you know a percent and the amount it represents, and need the original whole. Divide the part by the percent written as a decimal: if 25% of a number is 20, the whole is 20 divided by 0.25, which is 80.
objectives: Find the whole given a part and its percent.
Set up the division correctly.
Check the answer by taking the percent of the result.

skills.title: Finding the Percent
skills.summary: To find what percent one number is of another, divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100. For example, 15 out of 60 is 15 divided by 60 = 0.25, which is 25%.
objectives: Find what percent one number is of another.
Convert the resulting decimal to a percent.
Apply the method to scores and shares.

skills.title: Percent Increase and Decrease
skills.summary: A percent increase adds a percent of the original to itself, and a percent decrease subtracts it. To find the new amount, work out the change and add or subtract it, or multiply by 1 plus (or minus) the percent as a decimal.
objectives: Compute a percent increase.
Compute a percent decrease.
Find a sale price or an increased amount in one step.

skills.title: Percentage Word Problems
skills.summary: Percentage word problems describe real situations such as discounts, tips, taxes, and test scores. The key step is deciding which of the three percent questions is being asked: a percent of a number, what percent one number is of another, or the original whole.
objectives: Identify which percent calculation a word problem needs.
Solve real percent problems.
Check that the answer is reasonable.

components.body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to name decimal places, give the value of a digit after the decimal point, and connect decimals to fractions of ten and a hundred.
Recall that in a whole number, each place is ten times the place to its right: ones, tens, hundreds. A fraction names equal parts of one whole. Decimals extend place value to parts of one.

Imagine one whole split into 10 equal strips. Each strip is one tenth, written 0.1. Split one of those strips into 10 again and each tiny piece is one hundredth, written 0.01. The decimal point marks where whole ones end and parts of a whole begin.
The places after the decimal point are, in order, tenths, hundredths, and thousandths. A digit's value is the digit times its place. In 0.36, the 3 means 3 tenths and the 6 means 6 hundredths.

Picture a hundred-square (a 10 by 10 grid) that stands for one whole. One column of 10 shaded is one tenth, 0.1. One small cell shaded is one hundredth, 0.01. So 0.36 shades 3 full columns and 6 extra cells.

What is the value of the 5 in 0.257? The first place after the point is tenths (2), the second is hundredths (5), the third is thousandths (7). So the 5 is in the hundredths place and means 5 hundredths, or 5/100.
In 0.8, how many tenths are there? The digit 8 sits in the tenths place, so there are 8 tenths, and 0.8 equals 8/10.
A common mistake is thinking the first place after the point is hundredths. It is tenths. Another is reading 0.5 as five hundredths; it is five tenths, the same as 1/2.

The places after the decimal point are tenths, hundredths, and thousandths, each one tenth of the place before it. A digit's value is the digit times its place, and any decimal can be written as a fraction over 10, 100, or 1000.
In the number 0.47, what is the value of the 4 and the value of the 7?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to read decimals correctly and compare them by looking at place values, without being fooled by how many digits they have.
Recall the decimal places: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. Recall that with whole numbers you compare starting from the largest place on the left.

Think of money. $0.7 of a dollar is 70 cents, and $0.70 is also 70 cents, so they are equal; the extra 0 just fills the empty hundredths place. When comparing, 0.5 (fifty cents) is more than 0.45 (forty-five cents), even though 0.45 has more digits.

To compare decimals, line up the decimal points and compare digits from left to right, one place at a time. The first place where the digits differ decides which decimal is larger. Adding zeros to the right of the last digit does not change the value.
On a number line from 0 to 1 split into tenths, 0.5 sits halfway. The value 0.45 sits just before it, between 0.4 and 0.5, so 0.5 is clearly farther right and therefore greater.
Which is greater, 0.5 or 0.45? Compare the tenths place first: 0.5 has 5 tenths, 0.45 has 4 tenths. Since 5 tenths is more than 4 tenths, 0.5 is greater, even though 0.45 has more digits.
Compare 0.6 and 0.60. Write 0.6 as 0.60 by adding a zero in the hundredths place. Now both are 60 hundredths, so they are equal.
The most common mistake is thinking a decimal with more digits is larger (the 'longer is larger' error), such as saying 0.45 is greater than 0.5. Compare place by place from the left instead.
Read decimals with place-value names and compare them digit by digit from the left. Trailing zeros do not change value, so 0.7 equals 0.70, and more digits does not mean a larger number.
Why is 0.5 greater than 0.45 even though 0.45 has more digits?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to move between fractions and decimals for common values and explain why they name the same amount.
Recall that decimals are fractions over 10, 100, or 1000, and that you make an equivalent fraction by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number.

Half of a whole can be written as 1/2 or as 0.5, and both mean the same amount: five tenths. A decimal is just a fraction whose denominator is 10, 100, or 1000, so converting is about rewriting the fraction with one of those denominators.

To convert a fraction to a decimal, rewrite it as an equivalent fraction with denominator 10, 100, or 1000, then read off the digits; or divide the numerator by the denominator. To convert a decimal to a fraction, write it over its place value and simplify.
A hundred-square shows this well: 1/4 shades 25 of the 100 cells, which is 25 hundredths, or 0.25. The same square shows 1/2 as 50 cells, or 0.50.
Write 3/4 as a decimal. Make an equivalent fraction with denominator 100: multiply top and bottom by 25 to get 75/100. Seventy-five hundredths is 0.75. (You could also divide 3 by 4 to get 0.75.)
Write 1/5 as a decimal. Multiply top and bottom by 2 to get 2/10, which is two tenths, or 0.2.
A common mistake is writing 1/4 as 0.4 by just copying the digits. Instead, convert to hundredths: 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25. Another is forgetting to simplify, such as leaving 0.5 as 5/10 instead of 1/2.
Fractions and decimals can name the same amount. Convert a fraction by rewriting it over 10, 100, or 1000 (or by dividing), and convert a decimal by writing it over its place value and simplifying.
How can you turn 3/4 into a decimal, and what decimal do you get?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to add and subtract decimals by lining up the decimal points, and say why that step matters.
Recall that you can only combine amounts of the same size, and that decimal places are tenths, hundredths, and thousandths. You will also use multi-digit addition and subtraction.

Money makes this natural: to add $1.20 and $0.35 you add the cents to the cents and the dollars to the dollars. Lining up the decimal points keeps tenths with tenths and hundredths with hundredths, so you are combining pieces of the same size.

To add or subtract decimals, write the numbers so the decimal points are directly above each other, filling empty places with zeros. Add or subtract place by place, then bring the decimal point straight down into the answer.
Stack the numbers vertically with the decimal points aligned. For 1.2 + 0.35, write 1.20 above 0.35 so both have two decimal places, then add columns from the right: 1.20 + 0.35 = 1.55.
Add 3.46 + 2.7. Line up the points and write 2.7 as 2.70. Add hundredths: 6 + 0 = 6. Add tenths: 4 + 7 = 11, write 1 and carry 1. Add ones: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. The result is 6.16.
Subtract 0.9 - 0.3. The points are aligned and both are tenths. Subtract the tenths: 9 - 3 = 6, giving 0.6.
The most common mistake is lining up the last digits instead of the decimal points, which mixes tenths with hundredths. Always align the decimal points first, using zeros to fill empty places.
To add or subtract decimals, align the decimal points, fill empty places with zeros, combine place by place, and bring the decimal point straight down.
When adding 4.5 + 0.35, what must you line up, and why?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to multiply and divide decimals and place the decimal point correctly in the answer.
Recall your multiplication and division facts and that decimal places are tenths, hundredths, and thousandths. You will also use adding and subtracting decimals to check answers.

Multiplying 0.3 by 0.2 means taking 3 tenths of 2 tenths. Tenths times tenths gives hundredths, so the answer is in hundredths: 6 hundredths, or 0.06. Counting decimal places keeps track of how small the pieces get.

To multiply decimals, ignore the points and multiply the whole numbers, then give the answer the same total number of decimal places as the two factors together. To divide a decimal by a whole number, divide normally and bring the decimal point straight up into the quotient.
For 0.3 times 0.2, a hundred-square shows a rectangle 3 tenths wide and 2 tenths tall, covering 6 of the 100 small cells, which is 0.06.
Multiply 0.4 times 0.7. Multiply 4 times 7 to get 28. Each factor has 1 decimal place, so the answer has 2 decimal places: 0.28.
Divide 0.6 by 2. Think 6 tenths shared into 2 equal groups is 3 tenths, so 0.6 divided by 2 is 0.3.
A common mistake is forgetting to count decimal places when multiplying, writing 0.3 times 0.2 as 0.6 instead of 0.06. Count the decimal places in both factors and give the answer that many.
Multiply decimals as whole numbers, then place the point using the total decimal places of the factors. To divide by a whole number, divide as usual and bring the decimal point straight up.
In 0.4 times 0.7, how many decimal places should the answer have, and why?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain what percent means and convert between percents, fractions over 100, and decimals.
Recall that a decimal is a fraction over 10, 100, or 1000, and that 0.25 means 25 hundredths. Percent builds directly on hundredths.

Percent is just a special name for hundredths. If a test is scored out of 100 and you get 80 right, you scored 80 per hundred, or 80%. Because a percent is always out of 100, 80% is the same as 80/100 and the decimal 0.80.
Percent means per hundred; the symbol is %. To write a percent as a decimal, divide by 100 (move the point two places left): 25% = 0.25. To write a decimal as a percent, multiply by 100: 0.5 = 50%.
A hundred-square is a percent picture: each small cell is 1%. Shading 25 cells shows 25%, which is 25/100 of the square, or 0.25.
Write 7% as a decimal. Percent means out of 100, so 7% is 7/100. Seven hundredths is 0.07 (a zero is needed in the tenths place).
Write 0.5 as a percent. Multiply by 100: 0.5 times 100 is 50, so 0.5 is 50%.

A common mistake is writing 7% as 0.7 by moving the point only one place. Percent is out of 100, so move two places: 7% = 0.07. Another is thinking 100% is more than the whole; 100% is exactly the whole.
Percent means per hundred. A percent equals a fraction over 100 and a decimal found by dividing by 100. To turn a decimal into a percent, multiply by 100.
Why is 7% equal to 0.07 rather than 0.7?

lessons.title: Finding a Percent of a Number

components.body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to find a percent of a number by converting the percent to a decimal and multiplying, including in real situations.
Recall that a percent is out of 100, so 25% = 0.25, and that you can multiply a decimal by a whole number. Both ideas combine here.
Finding 25% of 80 means finding a quarter of 80, because 25% is 1/4. A quarter of 80 is 20. Turning the percent into a decimal or fraction lets you multiply to find any percent of any number.
To find a percent of a number, convert the percent to a decimal by dividing by 100, then multiply by the number. In symbols, percent of a number = (percent / 100) times the number.
Think of the number as a bar. Finding 20% means taking 20 of every 100 parts of the bar. For 45, that is 0.20 times 45, which is 9.
Find 25% of 80. Write 25% as 0.25. Multiply: 0.25 times 80 is 20. So 25% of 80 is 20. (Check: 25% is 1/4, and a quarter of 80 is 20.)
Find 10% of 50. Write 10% as 0.1 and multiply: 0.1 times 50 is 5. So 10% of 50 is 5.
A common mistake is multiplying by the percent number itself, such as 25 times 80, instead of by its decimal form 0.25. Always convert the percent to a decimal (divide by 100) first.
To find a percent of a number, change the percent to a decimal by dividing by 100, then multiply by the number. This calculates discounts, tips, and shares of a total.
How do you find 30% of a number, and by what decimal do you multiply?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to convert freely among fractions, decimals, and percents and use that to compare values.
Recall that a percent is out of 100, that a decimal is a fraction over 10 or 100, and how to convert common fractions to decimals. This lesson ties all three together.

One half can be written as 1/2, 0.5, or 50%. They are the same amount dressed in different clothes. Percent connects to decimals through hundredths, and decimals connect to fractions through place value, so all three link up.

Decimal to percent: multiply by 100 and add %. Percent to decimal: divide by 100. Percent to fraction: write over 100 and simplify. Fraction to decimal: rewrite over 10 or 100, or divide the numerator by the denominator.
A hundred-square ties them together: 50 shaded cells is 50/100 of the square, which is 50%, which is 0.50. The single picture shows all three forms at once.
Write 3/5 as a percent. First convert to a decimal: 3/5 = 6/10 = 0.6. Then convert the decimal to a percent by multiplying by 100: 0.6 times 100 is 60, so 3/5 is 60%.
Write 0.75 as a percent. Multiply by 100: 0.75 times 100 is 75, so 0.75 is 75%.

A common mistake is converting only part way, such as writing 3/5 as 0.6 but forgetting to multiply by 100 for the percent. Another is mixing up the direction: multiply by 100 to make a percent, divide by 100 to undo one.

Fractions, decimals, and percents are interchangeable. Multiply a decimal by 100 for a percent, divide a percent by 100 for a decimal, write a percent over 100 for a fraction, and divide a fraction for a decimal.
Starting from the fraction 3/5, what steps turn it into a percent, and what percent do you get?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to round decimals to the nearest whole number, tenth, or hundredth.
Recall rounding whole numbers and the decimal places: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

On a number line, 3.7 sits between 3 and 4 but is closer to 4, so rounding to the nearest whole number gives 4. The digit right after the rounding place tells you which side you are closer to, and 5 is the agreed tipping point where we round up.

To round to a given place, look at the digit immediately to its right. If that digit is 5 or greater, increase the rounding digit by one; otherwise leave it unchanged. Then drop all digits to the right of the rounding place.
Picture a number line from 3 to 4 divided into tenths. The halfway mark is 3.5. Anything at or above 3.5 rounds to 4; anything below rounds to 3.
Round 3.68 to the nearest tenth. The tenths digit is 6, and the digit to its right is 8. Since 8 is 5 or more, round the 6 up to 7, giving 3.7.
Round 2.4 to the nearest whole number. The digit after the ones place is 4, which is less than 5, so the answer stays 2.
A common mistake is looking at the wrong digit, or rounding one place at a time from the far right. Use only the single digit immediately to the right of the rounding place.
Round by checking the digit just right of the rounding place: 5 or more rounds up, less than 5 leaves the digit unchanged. Then drop the remaining digits.
When rounding 3.68 to the nearest tenth, which digit do you check, and what is the answer?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to find the original whole when you know a part and what percent it is.
Recall that finding a percent of a number multiplies by the percent as a decimal. This lesson reverses that step.
If 25% of a class is 6 students, then 6 people make up a quarter of the class, so the whole class is four times as big: 24. Undoing a multiplication means dividing.
If a part equals a given percent of an unknown whole, then whole = part divided by (percent / 100). Checking is easy: take that percent of your answer and confirm you get the part back.
25% of a number is 20. What is the number? Write 25% as 0.25 and divide: 20 divided by 0.25 = 80. Check: 0.25 times 80 = 20, correct.
50% of a number is 15. Divide: 15 divided by 0.5 = 30. Check: half of 30 is 15.
A common mistake is multiplying by the percent instead of dividing. If the part is smaller than the whole, the whole must be larger than the part, so division is the right move.
To find the whole, divide the part by the percent expressed as a decimal, then check by taking that percent of your answer.
If 25% of a number is 20, how do you find the number, and what is it?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to work out what percent one quantity is of another.
Recall that a percent is a fraction out of 100, and that multiplying a decimal by 100 turns it into a percent.
Scoring 15 out of 60 on a test, the fraction 15/60 tells you how much you got. Turning that fraction into a decimal and then into hundredths tells you the score as a percent: 25%.
To find what percent a part is of a whole, compute part divided by whole, then multiply by 100 and add the percent sign: percent = (part / whole) times 100.
What percent of 60 is 15? Divide: 15 / 60 = 0.25. Multiply by 100: 25. So 15 is 25% of 60.
What percent of 50 is 10? Divide: 10 / 50 = 0.2. Times 100 gives 20%.
A common mistake is dividing the wrong way round. The part goes on top; if your answer is above 100% but the part is smaller than the whole, you have divided upside down.
Percent = (part divided by whole) times 100. Divide the part by the whole first, then convert the decimal to a percent.
How do you work out what percent 15 is of 60?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to find new amounts after a percent increase or decrease.
Recall finding a percent of a number by multiplying by the percent as a decimal.
A $50 coat with 20% off loses $10, leaving $40. You can do this in two steps (find the discount, then subtract) or in one (pay 80% of the price, since 100% - 20% = 80%). Both give the same answer.

For a percent increase, new amount = original + (percent/100) times original, which equals original times (1 + percent/100). For a percent decrease, subtract instead: original times (1 - percent/100).
A $50 item is reduced by 20%. The discount is 0.2 times 50 = $10, so the new price is 50 - 10 = $40. In one step: 0.8 times 50 = $40.
A $200 salary rises by 10%. The increase is 0.1 times 200 = $20, so the new amount is $220. In one step: 1.1 times 200 = 220.
A common mistake is reporting the change instead of the new amount. If a $50 item drops 20%, the answer to 'what is the new price' is $40, not the $10 discount.
Percent increase multiplies by (1 + percent as a decimal); percent decrease multiplies by (1 - percent as a decimal). Or find the change and add or subtract it.
What are the two ways to find the price of a $50 item after a 20% discount?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to recognize and solve the three main kinds of percent word problem.
Recall the three tools: percent of a number (multiply), what percent one is of another (divide part by whole, times 100), and finding the whole (divide part by the percent).
Every percent problem gives you two of these three things - the percent, the part, and the whole - and asks for the third. Working out which one is missing tells you immediately what to do.

If the percent and whole are known, multiply to get the part. If the part and whole are known, divide part by whole and multiply by 100 to get the percent. If the part and percent are known, divide to get the whole.
A restaurant bill is $40 and you leave an 18% tip. The percent and whole are known, so multiply: 0.18 times 40 = $7.20 tip.
You got 45 of 50 questions right. The part and whole are known, so divide: 45 / 50 = 0.9, which is 90%.
A common mistake is applying the wrong operation because the numbers were not sorted into percent, part, and whole first. Identify what is missing before calculating.
Sort a percent word problem into percent, part, and whole, see which is missing, and use the matching method: multiply, divide-and-times-100, or divide.
What three quantities appear in every percent problem, and how do you know which method to use?

questions.prompt: In the number 3.4, which place is the digit 4 in?

hints.text: The first place to the right of the decimal point.

questions.explanation: The first place after the decimal point is the tenths place, so the 4 in 3.4 means 4 tenths.

questions.prompt: How many tenths are in 0.6?

hints.text: The digit after the decimal point counts tenths.
The digit is 6, so there are 6 tenths.

questions.explanation: 0.6 means 6 tenths, so there are 6 tenths and 0.6 equals 6/10.

questions.prompt: Write 0.9 as a fraction in simplest form.

hints.text: 9 and 10 share no common factor, so it is already simplest.

questions.explanation: 0.9 is 9 tenths, written 9/10, which is already in simplest form.

questions.prompt: What is the value of the digit 5 in 0.25?

hints.text: The second place after the point is hundredths.

questions.explanation: In 0.25 the 2 is in the tenths place and the 5 is in the hundredths place, so the 5 means 5 hundredths.

questions.prompt: Write 0.07 as a fraction in simplest form.

hints.text: The 7 is in the hundredths place.

questions.explanation: 0.07 has a 0 in the tenths place and a 7 in the hundredths place, so it is 7 hundredths, or 7/100.

questions.prompt: In the number 0.583, which digit is in the hundredths place?

hints.text: Tenths is first, hundredths is second.
The second digit after the point is 8.

questions.explanation: After the point the places are tenths (5), hundredths (8), thousandths (3), so the hundredths digit is 8.

questions.prompt: Write the decimal that means 4 tenths and 3 hundredths.

hints.text: Put the tenths digit first, then the hundredths digit.

questions.explanation: 4 tenths goes in the first place and 3 hundredths in the second place, giving 0.43.

questions.prompt: Write 6 hundredths as a decimal.

hints.text: Hundredths is the second place after the point.
There are no tenths, so put a 0 in the tenths place: 0.06.

questions.explanation: Six hundredths needs the hundredths (second) place, with a 0 in the tenths place to hold it: 0.06.

questions.prompt: Which fraction is equal to 0.5?

hints.text: 5/10 simplifies by dividing top and bottom by 5.

questions.explanation: 0.5 is 5 tenths, or 5/10, which simplifies to 1/2.

questions.prompt: Order these decimal places from largest to smallest. Arrange: tenths, thousandths, hundredths.

hints.text: Each place is one tenth the size of the place to its left.
Tenths are biggest, then hundredths, then thousandths.

questions.explanation: Moving right, each place is ten times smaller, so tenths are largest, then hundredths, then thousandths.

questions.prompt: Which statement about 0.7 and 0.70 is true?

hints.text: Add a zero to 0.7 in the hundredths place.
0.70 is 70 hundredths and 0.7 is 7 tenths, which is also 70 hundredths.

questions.explanation: 0.7 equals 0.70 because a trailing zero fills the empty hundredths place without changing the value.

questions.prompt: Which decimal is greater, 0.5 or 0.45?
questions.explanation: The tenths digit decides it: 5 tenths is more than 4 tenths, so 0.5 is greater.

questions.prompt: Which decimal is smaller, 0.3 or 0.29?

hints.text: 0.29 has fewer tenths, so it is smaller.

questions.explanation: 0.3 has 3 tenths and 0.29 has 2 tenths, so 0.29 is smaller despite having more digits.

questions.prompt: Order these from least to greatest. Arrange: 0.4, 0.04, 0.44.

hints.text: 0.04 has 0 tenths, 0.4 and 0.44 have 4 tenths; then compare hundredths.

questions.explanation: 0.04 has 0 tenths so it is least; 0.4 and 0.44 both have 4 tenths, and 0.44 has extra hundredths, so 0.44 is greatest.

questions.prompt: Which symbol makes this true: 0.6 __ 0.60 ?
questions.explanation: 0.6 and 0.60 are both 60 hundredths, so the correct symbol is the equals sign.

questions.prompt: Which decimal is the greatest: 0.812, 0.9, 0.85, or 0.088?

hints.text: Compare the tenths place across all four.
0.9 has 9 tenths, the most of any option.

questions.explanation: Comparing tenths first, 0.9 has 9 tenths while the others have 8 or 0 tenths, so 0.9 is greatest.

questions.prompt: Order these from least to greatest. Arrange: 0.5, 0.55, 0.505, 0.05.

hints.text: Compare tenths first, then hundredths, then thousandths.
0.05 has 0 tenths; among the 5-tenths values compare the next places.

questions.explanation: 0.05 has 0 tenths so it is least; the rest have 5 tenths, then 0.5 (=0.500) < 0.505 < 0.55 by the later places.

questions.prompt: How do you read 0.25 using place-value names?

hints.text: The last digit is in the hundredths place.

questions.explanation: 0.25 has its last digit in the hundredths place, so it is read as twenty-five hundredths (which equals 1/4).

questions.prompt: Select every value that is equal to 0.3. Enter your choices separated by | (for example: A|B).

hints.text: Trailing zeros do not change value.
0.03 is only 3 hundredths, which is different.

questions.explanation: 0.30, 0.300, and 3/10 all equal 3 tenths; 0.03 is 3 hundredths, which is ten times smaller.

questions.prompt: One runner ran 0.400 km and another ran 0.4 km. Who ran farther?

hints.text: Trailing zeros do not change the value.
